entries.4148bbf016a44b867366f4df8cc085d6cd4a06b0: <div sID="gen20176" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Amos.6" sID="Amos.6"/> <div eID="gen20176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20177" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20178" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A sinful people studying to put a slight upon God's threatenings and to make them appear trivial, confiding in their privileges and pre-eminences above other nations (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.2-Amos.6.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>), and their power (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.13">ver. 13</reference>), and wholly addicted to their pleasures, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4-Amos.6.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. II. A serious prophet studying to put a weight upon God's threatenings and to make them appear terrible, by setting forth the severity of those judgments that were coming upon these sensualists (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.7">ver. 7</reference>), God's abhorring them, and abandoning them and theirs to death (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.8-Amos.6.11">ver. 8-11</reference>), and bringing utter desolation upon them, since they would not be wrought upon by the methods he had taken for their conviction, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.12-Amos.6.14">ver. 12-14</reference>.
entries.a45f41f817404a241b5cb47c9e4df66adf79d8dd: <div eID="gen20178" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20177" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Danger of False Security. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20179" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Woe to them <hi type="italic">that are</hi> at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, <hi type="italic">which are</hi> named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came! <hi type="super">2</hi> Pass ye unto Calneh, and see; and from thence go ye to Hamath the great: then go down to Gath of the Philistines: <hi type="italic">be they</hi> better than these kingdoms? or their border greater than your border? <hi type="super">3</hi> Ye that put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of violence to come near; <hi type="super">4</hi> That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall; <hi type="super">5</hi> That chant to the sound of the viol, <hi type="italic">and</hi> invent to themselves instruments of music, like David; <hi type="super">6</hi> That drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph. <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore now shall they go captive with the first that go captive, and the banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed. <div eID="gen20179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20180" type="x-p"/> The first words of the chapter are the contents of these verses; but they sound very strangely, and contrary to the sentiments of a vain world: <hi type="italic">Woe to those that are at ease!</hi> We are ready to say, <hi type="italic">Happy are those that are at ease,</hi> that neither feel any trouble nor fear any, that lie soft and warm, and lay nothing to heart; and wise we think are those that do so, that bathe themselves in the delights of sense and care not how the world goes. Those are looked upon as doing well for themselves that do well for their bodies and make much of them; but against them this woe is denounced, and we are here told what their ease is, and what the woe is. <div eID="gen20180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20181" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a description of their pride, security, and sensuality, for which God would reckon with them. <div eID="gen20181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20182" type="x-p"/> 1. They were vainly conceited of their own dignities, and thought those would secure them from the judgments threatened and be their defence against the wrath both of God and man. (1.) Those that dwelt in Zion thought that was honour and protection enough for them, and they might there be quiet from all fear of evil, because it was a strong city, well fortified both by nature and art (we read of Zion's <hi type="italic">strong-holds</hi> and her <hi type="italic">bulwarks</hi>), and because it was a royal city, where were set the thrones of the house of David (it was the head-city of Judah, and therefore truly great), and especially because it was the holy city, where the temple was, and the testimony of Israel; those that dwelt there doubted not but that God's sanctuary would be a sanctuary to them and would shelter them from his judgments. The <hi type="italic">temple of the Lord are these,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jer. vii. 4</reference>. They are <hi type="italic">haughty because of the holy mountain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.11">Zeph. iii. 11</reference>. Note, Many are puffed up with pride, and rocked asleep in carnal security, by their church-privileges, and the place they have in Zion. (2.) Those that dwelt <hi type="italic">in the mountain of Samaria,</hi> though it was not a holy hill, like that of Zion, yet they trusted in it, because it was the metropolis of a potent kingdom, and perhaps, in imitation of Jerusalem, was the head-quarters of its religion; and by lapse of time the hill of Shemer became with them in as good repute as the hill of Zion ever was. They hoped for salvation from these hills and mountains. (3.) Both these two kingdoms valued themselves upon their relation to Israel, that prince with God, which they looked upon as masking them the <hi type="italic">chief of the nations,</hi> more ancient and honourable than any of them; the <hi type="italic">first-fruits of the nations</hi> (so the word is), dedicated to God and sanctifying the whole harvest. The <hi type="italic">house of Israel</hi> came to them, that is, was divided into those kingdoms, of which Zion and Samaria were the mother cities. Those that were at ease were the princes and rulers, the great men, that were <hi type="italic">chief of the nations,</hi> chief of those two kingdoms, and to whom, having their residence in Zion and Samaria, the whole house of Israel applied for judgment. Note, It is hard to be great and not to be proud. Great nations and great men are apt to overvalue themselves, and to overlook their neighbours, because they think they a little overtop them. But, for a check to their pride and security, the prophet bids them take notice of those cities that were within the compass of their knowledge, that had been as illustrious in their time as ever Zion or Samaria was, and yet were destroyed, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.2">v. 2</reference>. "Go <hi type="italic">to Calneh</hi> (which was an ancient city built by Nimrod, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">Gen. x. 10</reference>), and see what has become of that, it is now in ruins; so is <hi type="italic">Hamath the great,</hi> one of the chief cities of Syria. Sennacherib boasts of <hi type="italic">destroying the gods of Hamath.</hi> Gath was likewise made desolate by Hazael, and not long ago, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.12.17">2 Kings xii. 17</reference>. Now <hi type="italic">were they better than these kingdoms</hi> of Judah and Israel? Yes, they were, and <hi type="italic">their border greater than your border,</hi> so that they had more reason than you to be confident of their own safety; yet you see what has become of them, and dare you be secure? <hi type="italic">Art thou better than populous No?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8">Nah. iii. 8</reference>. Note, The examples of others' ruin forbid us to be secure. <div eID="gen20182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20183" type="x-p"/> 2. They persisted in their wicked courses upon a presumption that they should never be called to an account for them (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You put far away the evil day,</hi> the day of reckoning, as a thing that shall never come, or you look upon it as at such a distance that it makes no impression at all upon you; you <hi type="italic">put it far away,</hi> and think you can still put it yet further, and adjourn it <hi type="italic">de die in diem—from day to day,</hi> and therefore you <hi type="italic">cause the seat of violence to draw near;</hi> you venture upon all acts of injustice and oppression, and have <hi type="italic">fellowship with the throne of iniquity, which frames mischief by a law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.94.20">Ps. xciv. 20</reference>. You cause that to come near, as if that would be your protection from these judgments which really ripens you for them." Note, <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> men take sin to be near them, because they take judgment to be far off from them; but those deceive themselves who thus mock God. <div eID="gen20183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20184" type="x-p"/> 3. They indulged themselves in all manner of sensual pleasures and delights, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4-Amos.6.6">v. 4-6</reference>. These Israelites were perfect epicures and slaves to their appetites. Their dignities (in consideration of which they ought to have been examples of self-denial and mortification), they thought, would justify them in their sensuality; the gains of their oppression and violence, they thought, would bear the charge of it; and they put the evil day at a distance, that they might give them no disturbance in it. That which they are here charged with is not in itself sinful (these things might be soberly and moderately used), but they placed their happiness in the gratification of their carnal appetites; and though they were men in office, that had business to mind, they gave themselves up to their pleasures, spent their time in them, and threw away their thoughts, and cares, and estates upon them. They were in these enjoyments as in their element. Their hearts were upon them; they exceeded all bounds in them, and this at a time when God in his providence was calling them to <hi type="italic">weeping and mourning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.12-Isa.22.13">Isa. xxii. 12, 13</reference>. When they were under guilt and wrath, and the judgments of God were ready to break in upon them, they called for <hi type="italic">wine and strong drink,</hi> presuming that <hi type="italic">to-morrow shall be as this day, and much more abundant</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.12">Isa. lvi. 12</reference>), thus walking contrary to God and setting his justice at defiance. (1.) They were extravagant in their furniture. Nothing would serve them but <hi type="italic">beds of ivory</hi> to sleep upon, or to sit on at their meat, when sackcloth and ashes would have become them better. (2.) They were lazy, and humoured themselves in the love of ease. They did not only lie down, but <hi type="italic">stretched themselves</hi> upon their couches, when they should have stirred up themselves to their business; they were willingly slothful, and took a pride in doing nothing; they <hi type="italic">abound in superfluities</hi> (so the margin reads it), when many of their poor brethren wanted necessaries. (3.) They were nice and curious in their diet, must have every thing of the best and abundance of it: They ate <hi type="italic">the lambs out of the flock</hi> (lambs by wholesale) and the <hi type="italic">calves out of the midst of the stall,</hi> the fattest they could lay their hand on; and these perhaps not out of their own flock and their own stall, but taken by oppression from the poor. (4.) They were merry and jovial, and diverted themselves at their feasts with music and singing: They <hi type="italic">chant to the sound of the viol,</hi> sing and play in concert, and they invent new-fashioned <hi type="italic">instruments of music,</hi> striving herein, more than in any thing else, to excel their ancestors; they set their wits on work to contrive how to please their fancy. Some men never show their ingenuity but in their luxury; on that they bestow all their faculty of invention and contrivance. They invent <hi type="italic">instruments of music, like David,</hi> entertain themselves with that which formerly used to be the entertainment of kings only. Or it intimates their profaneness in their mirth; they mimicked the temple-music, and made a jest of that, because, it may be, it was old-fashioned, and they took a pride in bantering it as the Babylonians did when they urged the captives to sing to them the <hi type="italic">songs of Zion;</hi> such was Belshazzar's profaneness when he drank wine in temple-bowls, and such is theirs that sing vain and loose songs in psalm-tunes, on purpose to ridicule a divine institution. (5.) They drank to excess, and never thought they could pour down enough: They <hi type="italic">drank wink in bowls,</hi> not in glasses, or cups (as <reference osisRef="Jer.35.5">Jer. xxxv. 5</reference>); they hate to be stinted, and must have large draughts, and therefore make use of vessels that they can steal a draught out of. (6.) They affected the strongest perfumes: They <hi type="italic">anoint themselves with the chief ointments,</hi> to please the smell, and to make them more in love with their own bodies, and to guard against those presages of putrefaction which they carry about with them while they live. No ordinary ointments would serve their turn; they must have the chief, such as were far-fetched and dear-bought, when cheaper would have served as well. <div eID="gen20184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20185" type="x-p"/> 4. They had no concern at all for the interests of the church of God, and of the nation, that were sinking and going to decay: <hi type="italic">They are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph;</hi> the church of God, including both the kingdoms of Judah and Israel (which are called <hi type="italic">Joseph,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">Ps. lxxx. 1</reference>), was in distress, invaded, insulted, and broken in upon. As to their own kingdom which they were entrusted with the government of, the affairs of which they were directors of, the peace of which they were the conservators of, great breaches were made upon it, upon its peace and welfare; and they were so besotted that they were not aware of them, so indulgent of their pleasures that they never laid them to heart, and had such an aversion to the thing called business that they were in no care or concern to get them repaired. It is all one to them whether the nation sink or swim, so that they can but lie at ease and live in pleasure. Particular persons that belonged to Joseph were in affliction, and they took no cognizance of their case of the wrongs and hardships they sustained and the troubles they were in, nor took any care to relieve them, and right them, contrary to the temper of holy Job, who, when he was in prosperity, <hi type="italic">wept with him</hi> that <hi type="italic">was in misery</hi> and his <hi type="italic">soul was grieved for the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.25">Job xxx. 25</reference>. Some think that, in calling the afflicted church <hi type="italic">Joseph,</hi> there is an allusion to the story of Pharaoh's butler, who, when he preferred to give the cup again into his master's hand, <hi type="italic">remembered not Joseph, but forgot him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.40.21">Gen. xl. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.40.23">23</reference>. Thus they <hi type="italic">drank wine in bowls,</hi> but <hi type="italic">were not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.</hi> Note, Those are commonly careless of the troubles of others who are set upon their own pleasures; and it is a great offence to God when his church is in affliction and we are not grieved for it, nor lay it to heart. <div eID="gen20185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20186" type="x-p"/> II. Here is the doom passed upon them (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore now shall they go captive with the first that go captive,</hi> and shall fall into all the miseries that attend captives; and the <hi type="italic">banquet of those</hi> that <hi type="italic">stretched themselves</hi> upon their couches <hi type="italic">shall be removed.</hi> Their plenty shall be taken from them, and they from it, because they made it the food and fuel of their lusts. 1. Those who lived in luxury shall lose even their liberty; and by being brought into servitude shall be justly punished for the abuse of their dignity and dominion. 2. Those who trusted in the delights and pleasures of their own land shall be carried away into a strange land, and so made ashamed of their pride and confidence; they shall <hi type="italic">go captive.</hi> 3. Those who placed their happiness in the pleasures of sense, and set their hearts upon them, shall be deprived of those pleasures; their banquet shall be removed, and they shall know what it is to fare hard. 4. Those who <hi type="italic">stretched themselves</hi> shall be made to contract themselves, and to come into a less compass. 5. Those who <hi type="italic">put the evil day far from them</hi> shall find it nearer to them than it is to others; <hi type="italic">those shall go captive with the first</hi> who flattered themselves with hopes that if trouble did come they should be the last who should be seized by it. Those are ripening apace for trouble themselves who lay not to heart the trouble of others and of the church of God. Those who give themselves to mirth, when God calls them to mourning, will find it a sin that shall not go unpunished, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.14">Isa. xxii. 14</reference>.
entries.e56f47278ff319b831e7a3d0ec7fcc340457bda0: <div eID="gen20186" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings of Judgment. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20187" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> hath sworn by himself, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> the God of hosts, I abhor the excellency of Jacob, and hate his palaces: therefore will I deliver up the city with all that is therein. <hi type="super">9</hi> And it shall come to pass, if there remain ten men in one house, that they shall die. <hi type="super">10</hi> And a man's uncle shall take him up, and he that burneth him, to bring out the bones out of the house, and shall say unto him that <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the sides of the house, <hi type="italic">Is there</hi> yet <hi type="italic">any</hi> with thee? and he shall say, No. Then shall he say, Hold thy tongue: for we may not make mention of the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">11</hi> For, behold, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commandeth, and he will smite the great house with breaches, and the little house with clefts. <hi type="super">12</hi> Shall horses run upon the rock? will <hi type="italic">one</hi> plow <hi type="italic">there</hi> with oxen? for ye have turned judgment into gall, and the fruit of righteousness into hemlock: <hi type="super">13</hi> Ye which rejoice in a thing of nought, which say, Have we not taken to us horns by our own strength? <hi type="super">14</hi> But, behold, I will raise up against you a nation, O house of Israel, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> the God of hosts; and they shall afflict you from the entering in of Hemath unto the river of the wilderness. <div eID="gen20187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20188" type="x-p"/> In the former part of the chapter we had these secure Israelites loading themselves with pleasures, as if they could never be made merry enough; here we have God loading them with punishments, as if they could never be made miserable enough. And observe, <div eID="gen20188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20189" type="x-p"/> I. How strongly this burden is bound on, not to be shaken off by their presumption and security; for it is bound by <hi type="italic">the Lord the God of hosts,</hi> by his mighty, his almighty, hand, which none can resist; it is bound with an oath, which puts the sentence past revocation: <hi type="italic">The Lord God has sworn, and he will not repent,</hi> and, since he could swear by no greater, he has sworn by himself. How dreadful, how miserable, is the case of those whose ruin, whose eternal ruin, God himself has sworn, who can execute his purpose and cannot alter it! <div eID="gen20189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20190" type="x-p"/> II. How heavily this burden lies! Let us see the particulars. 1. God will abhor and abandon them, and that implies misery enough, all misery: <hi type="italic">I abhor the excellency of Jacob,</hi> all that which they are proud of, and value themselves upon, and for which they call and count themselves the <hi type="italic">chief of nations.</hi> Their visible church-membership, and the privileges of that, their temple, altar, and priesthood, these were, more than any thing, the excellencies of Jacob; but, when these were profaned and polluted by sin, God abhorred them; he hated and despised them, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.21">ch. v. 21</reference>. Note, God abhors that form of godliness which hypocrites keep up, while they abhor the power of it. And if he abhors their temple, for the iniquity of that, no marvel that he hates their palaces, for the injustices and oppression he finds there. Note, that creature which we take such a complacency and put such a confidence in as to make it a rival with God is thereby made abominable to him. He <hi type="italic">hates the palaces</hi> of sinners, for the sake of wickedness of those that dwell therein. <reference osisRef="Prov.3.33">Prov. iii. 33</reference>, <hi type="italic">The curse of the Lord is in the house of the wicked.</hi> And, if God abhor them, immediately it follows, He will <hi type="italic">deliver up the city with all that is therein,</hi> deliver it up into the hands of the enemy, that will lay it waste, and make a prey of all its wealth. Note, Those that are abhorred and abandoned of God are undone to all intents and purposes. 2. There shall be a great and general mortality among them (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">If there remain ten men in one house,</hi> that have escaped the sword of the enemy, yet they shall be met with another way; <hi type="italic">they shall</hi> all <hi type="italic">die</hi> by famine or pestilence. In the most sickly times, if there be ten in a house, one may hope that at least the one-half of them will escape, according to the proportion of two in a bed, <hi type="italic">one taken and the other left;</hi> but here not one of ten shall live to bury the rest. Another instance of the greatness of the mortality is (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.10">v. 10</reference>) that the nearest relations of the dead shall be forced with their own hands to wind up their bodies, and bury them, for want of other hands to be employed in it; that is all that the <hi type="italic">next of kin,</hi> to whom the right of redemption belongs, can do for them, and with great reluctance will they do that. It intimates that the young people shall be cut off soonest; for the uncle that survives is, ordinarily, the senior relation. "When the uncle comes with the sexton (or <hi type="italic">him that burns</hi>), <hi type="italic">to bring out the bones out of the house,</hi> he <hi type="italic">shall say</hi> to him that he sees next about the house, '<hi type="italic">Is there any yet with thee?</hi> Are there any left alive?' And he shall say, 'No, this is the last; now the whole family is cut off by death, and neither root nor branch remains.'" But that which makes the judgment the more grievous is that their hearts seem to be hardened under it. "When he that is found by the sides of the house begin to enter into discourse with those that are carrying off the dead, they shall say, '<hi type="italic">Hold thy tongue;</hi> do not stand preaching to us about the hand of Providence in this calamity, for <hi type="italic">we may not make mention of the name of the Lord;</hi> God is so angry with us that there is no speaking to him; he is so extreme to mark what we do amiss that we dare not so much as make mention of his name." ' Thus <hi type="italic">the foolishness of men perverts their way,</hi> and brings them into distress, and then <hi type="italic">their heart frets against the Lord.</hi> Even then they will not take notice of his hand, nor suffer those about them to do it. Perhaps it was forbidden by some of the idolatrous kings to make mention of the name of <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> as by the law of Moses it was forbidden to make mention of the names of the heathen-gods: "We may not do it without incurring the penalty." Note, Those hearts are wretchedly hardened indeed that will not be brought to make mention of God's name, and to worship him, when the hand of God has gone out against them, and when, as here, sickness and death are in their families. Thus those <hi type="italic">heap up wrath</hi> who <hi type="italic">cry not when God binds them.</hi> 3. Their houses shall be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.11">v. 11</reference>. God <hi type="italic">will smite the great house with breaches, and the little house with clefts;</hi> they shall both be cracked so as to lose their beauty and strength, and to be hastening towards a fall. The princes' palaces are not above the rebuke of divine justice, nor the poor men's cottages beneath it; neither shall escape. When sin has marked them for ruin God will find ways to bring it about. It is by order from him that breaches are made. <div eID="gen20190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20191" type="x-p"/> III. How justly they are thus burdened. If we understand the matter aright, we shall say, <hi type="italic">The Lord is righteous.</hi> 1. The methods used for their reformation had been all fruitless and ineffectual (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Shall horses run upon the rock,</hi> to hurl or harrow the ground there? Or will <hi type="italic">one plough there with oxen?</hi> No, for there will be no profit to countervail the pains. God has sent them his prophets, to <hi type="italic">break up their fallow-ground;</hi> but they found them as hard and inflexible as the rock, rough and rugged, and they could do no good with them, nor work upon them, and therefore they shall not attempt it any more. They will not be reclaimed, and therefore shall not be reproved, but quite abandoned. Note, Those who will not be cultivated as fields and vineyards shall be rejected as barren rocks and deserts, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.7-Heb.6.8">Heb. vi. 7, 8</reference>. 2. They had abused their power to the wrong and oppression of many, whose injured cause the sovereign Judge would not only right, but revenge: <hi type="italic">You have turned judgment into gall,</hi> which is nauseous, and <hi type="italic">the fruit of righteousness into hemlock,</hi> which is noxious; it would make one sick to see how those that were entrusted with the administration of public justice bore down equity with that power which they out to have defended and supported it, and so turned its own artillery against itself. Note, When our services of God are soured with sin his providences will justly be embittered to us. 3. They had set the judgments of God at defiance, and, confiding in their own strength, thought themselves a match for Omnipotence, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.13">v. 13</reference>. They <hi type="italic">rejoiced in a thing of nought,</hi> pleased themselves with a fancy that no evil should befal them, though they had no ground at all for that confidence, nothing to trust to that would bear any weight. They said, "<hi type="italic">Have we not taken to us horns;</hi> have we not arrived to great dignity and dominion, have we not pushed down our enemies and pushed on our victories, and this <hi type="italic">by our own strength,</hi> our own skill and courage, our own wealth and military force? Who then need we be afraid of? Who then need we make court to? Not God himself." Note, Prosperity and success commonly make men secure and haughty; and those that have done much think they can do any thing, any thing without God, nay, any thing against him. But those who trust in their own strength rejoice in <hi type="italic">a thing of nought,</hi> and so they will find. Probably they did not say this with their lips, <hi type="italic">totidem verbis—in so many words,</hi> but it was the language of their hearts and of their actions, both which God understands. <div eID="gen20191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20192" type="x-p"/> IV. How easily and effectually this burden shall be brought upon them, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.14">v. 14</reference>. He that brings it upon them is <hi type="italic">the Lord the God of hosts,</hi> who both may do and can do what he pleases, who has all creatures at his command, and who, when he has work to do, will not be at a loss for instruments to do it with; though they are the house of Israel, yet he will <hi type="italic">raise up against them a nation</hi> which they feared not, but had many a time hoped in, even the Assyrians, and this nation shall <hi type="italic">afflict them,</hi> bring them into straits, and put them to pain, from the <hi type="italic">entering in of Hamath,</hi> in the north, to <hi type="italic">the river of the wilderness,</hi> the river of Egypt, Sihor or Nile, in the south. The whole nation has shared in the iniquity, and therefore must expect to share in the calamity. Note, When men are in any way instruments of affliction to us we must see God raising them up against us, for they are in his hand—the rod, the sword, in his hand. The Lord has bidden Shimei curse David.  <chapter eID="Amos.6"/> <div eID="gen20192" type="x-p"/>

entries.ef87104d6405a97725573c0e917cfdba4260d2cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12590"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Amos.6.1-Amos.6.14">Am 6:1-14</reference>. Denunciation of Both the Sister Nations (Especially Their Nobles) For Wanton Security--Zion, as Well as Samaria: Threat of the Exile: Ruin of Their Palaces and Slaughter of the People: Their Perverse Injustice.</title> <div sID="gen23212" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12590"/><hi type="bold">1. named chief of the nations--</hi>that is, you nobles, so eminent in influence, that your names are celebrated among the chief nations [Ludovicus De Dieu]. Hebrew, "Men designated by name among the first-fruits of the nations," that is, men of note in Israel, the people chosen by God as first of the nations (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Num.24.20">Nu 24:20</reference>) [Piscator].<div eID="gen23212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to whom ... Israel came--</hi>that is, the princes to whom the Israelites used to repair for the decision of controversies, recognizing their authority [Maurer]. I prefer to refer "which" to the antecedent "Zion" and "Samaria"; these were esteemed "chief" strongholds among the heathen nations "to whom ... Israel came" when it entered Canaan; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.2">Am 6:2</reference> accords with this. <div eID="gen23213" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4865eed792f5290725b25bbd33080bf3c785176: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12591"/><div sID="gen23214" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12591"/><hi type="bold">2. Calneh--</hi>on the east bank of the Tigris. Once powerful, but recently subjugated by Assyria (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.9">Is 10:9</reference>; about 794 B.C.).<div eID="gen23214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hameth--</hi>subjugated by Jeroboam II (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Ki 14:25</reference>). Also by Assyria subsequently (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.34">2Ki 18:34</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Amos.6.14">Am 6:14</reference>.<div eID="gen23215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gath--</hi>subjugated by Uzziah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.6">2Ch 26:6</reference>).<div eID="gen23216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be they better--</hi>no. Their so recent subjugation renders it needless for Me to tell you they are not. And yet they once were; still they could not defend themselves against the enemy. How vain, then, your secure confidence in the strength of Mounts Zion and Samaria! He takes cities respectively east, north, south, and west of Israel (compare <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8">Na 3:8</reference>). <div eID="gen23217" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c5acb602d2a3dd2778f06c7f1f1408f24688ec8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12592"/><div sID="gen23218" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12592"/>3. Ye persuade yourselves that "the evil day" foretold by the prophets is "far off," though they declare it near (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.22">Eze 12:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.27">27</reference>). Ye in your imagination put it far off, and therefore bring near violent oppression, suffering it to sit enthroned, as it were, among you (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.20">Psa 94:20</reference>). The notion of judgment being far off has always been an incentive to the sinner's recklessness of living (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">Ec 8:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.48">Mt 24:48</reference>). Yet that very recklessness brings near the evil day which he puts far off. "Ye bring on fever by your intemperance, and yet would put it far off" [Calvin]. <div eID="gen23218" type="x-p"/>
entries.916f9e7a3a7b381e2a6053a811f516b53239bd3e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12593"/><div sID="gen23219" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12593"/>4. (See <reference osisRef="Amos.2.8">Am 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen23219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23220" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beds of ivory--</hi>that is, adorned, or inlaid, with ivory (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.15">Am 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stretch themselves--</hi>in luxurious self-indulgence.<div eID="gen23221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23222" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lambs out of the flock--</hi>picked out as the choicest, for their owners' selfish gratification. <div eID="gen23222" type="x-p"/>
entries.1014c325ca76bd02f2c35330344b8f6771991e73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12594"/><div sID="gen23223" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12594"/><hi type="bold">5. chant--</hi>literally, "mark distinct sounds and tones."<div eID="gen23223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">viol--</hi>the lyre, or lute.<div eID="gen23224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">invent ... instruments ... like David--</hi>They fancy they equal David in musical skill (<reference osisRef="1Chr.23.5">1Ch 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.12.36">Ne 12:36</reference>). They defend their luxurious passion for music by his example: forgetting that he pursued this study when at peace and free from danger, and that for the praise of God; but they pursue for their own self-gratification, and that when God is angry and ruin is imminent. <div eID="gen23225" type="x-p"/>
entries.83e21e3d2b4d451bed1ad68e4531e969930f431c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12595"/><div sID="gen23226" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12595"/><hi type="bold">6. drink ... in bowls--</hi>in the large vessels or basins in which wine was mixed; not satisfied with the smaller cups from which it was ordinarily drunk, after having been poured from the large mixer.<div eID="gen23226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chief ointments--</hi>that is, the most costly: not for health or cleanliness, but wanton luxury.<div eID="gen23227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not grieved for the affliction of Joseph--</hi>literally, "the breach," that is, the national wound or calamity (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.2">Psa 60:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.4">Eze 34:4</reference>) of the house of Joseph (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.6">Am 5:6</reference>); resembling in this the heartlessness of their forefathers, the sons of Jacob, towards Joseph, "eating bread" while their brother lay in the pit, and then selling him to Ishmaelites. <div eID="gen23228" type="x-p"/>
entries.35a7ef6dc0b4114d7e8c0d37b7f19a2f6129b00c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12596"/><div sID="gen23229" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12596"/><hi type="bold">7. Therefore ... shall they go captive with the first--</hi>As they were first among the people in rank (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>), and anointed themselves "with the chief ointments" (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Am 6:6</reference>), so shall they be among the foremost in going into captivity.<div eID="gen23229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23230" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">banquet--</hi>literally, the "merry-making shout of revellers"; from an Arabic root, "to cry out." In the Hebrew, marzeach; here, there is an allusion to mizraqu, "bowls" (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Am 6:6</reference>).<div eID="gen23230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them that stretched themselves--</hi>on luxurious couches (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.4">Am 6:4</reference>). <div eID="gen23231" type="x-p"/>
entries.cba2200b18196a054edbafeb94344a1f7bb30e1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12597"/><div sID="gen23232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12597"/><hi type="bold">8. the excellency of Jacob--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.47.4">Psa 47:4</reference>). The sanctuary which was the great glory of the covenant-people [Vatablus], (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.21">Eze 24:21</reference>). The priesthood, and kingdom, and dignity, conferred on them by God. These, saith God, are of no account in My eyes towards averting punishment [Calvin].<div eID="gen23232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hate his palaces--</hi>as being the storehouses of "robbery" (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.10">Am 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.15">15</reference>). How sad a change from God's love of Zion's gates (<reference osisRef="Ps.87.2">Psa 87:2</reference>) and palaces (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.3">Psa 48:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.48.13">13</reference>), owing to the people's sin!<div eID="gen23233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the city--</hi>collectively: both Zion and Samaria (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>).<div eID="gen23234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all that is therein--</hi>literally, "its fulness"; the multitude of men and of riches in it (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1">Psa 24:1</reference>). <div eID="gen23235" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b360ad3f21552a3990f4c0246abf67976528455: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12598"/><div sID="gen23236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12598"/>9. If as many as ten (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.26">Le 26:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.8.23">Zec 8:23</reference>) remain in a house (a rare case, and only in the scattered villages, as there will be scarcely a house in which the enemy will leave any), they shall all, to a man, die of the plague, a frequent concomitant of war in the East (<reference osisRef="Jer.24.10">Jr 24:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.13">44:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.11">Eze 6:11</reference>). <div eID="gen23236" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e10edbf4d907161e7b8ecab50cc34717fa99f07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12599"/><div sID="gen23237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12599"/><hi type="bold">10. a man's uncle--</hi>The nearest relatives had the duty of burying the dead (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.9">Ge 25:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.29">35:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.16.31">Jud 16:31</reference>). No nearer relative was left of this man than an uncle.<div eID="gen23237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he that burneth him--</hi>the uncle, who is also at the same time the one that burneth him (one of the "ten," <reference osisRef="Amos.6.9">Am 6:9</reference>). Burial was the usual Hebrew mode of disposing of their dead. But in cases of necessity, as when the men of Jabesh-gilead took the bodies of Saul and his three sons from the walls of Beth-shan and burned them to save them from being insulted by the Philistines, burning was practised. So in this case, to prevent contagion.<div eID="gen23238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the bones--</hi>that is, the dead body (<reference osisRef="Gen.50.25">Ge 50:25</reference>). Perhaps here there is an allusion in the phrase to the emaciated condition of the body, which was little else but skin and bones.<div eID="gen23239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">say unto him that is by the sides of the house--</hi>that is, to the only one left of the ten in the interior of the house [Maurer] (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Is 14:13</reference>).<div eID="gen23240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hold thy tongue ... we may not ... mention ... the Lord--</hi>After receiving the reply, that none is left besides the one addressed, when the man outside fancies the man still surviving inside to be on the point, as was customary, of expressing devout gratitude to God who spared him, the man outside interrupts him, "Hold thy tongue! for there is not now cause for mentioning with praise (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.7">Jos 23:7</reference>) the name of Jehovah"; for thou also must die; as all the ten are to die to the last man (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.9">Am 6:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Amos.8.3">Am 8:3</reference>). Formerly ye boasted in the name of Jehovah, as if ye were His peculiar people; now ye shall be silent and shudder at His name, as hostile to you, and as one from whom ye wish to be hidden (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Re 6:16</reference>), [Calvin]. <div eID="gen23241" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b96baaa892e431e3b392678b7f6aed4f4bc4073: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12600"/><div sID="gen23242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12600"/><hi type="bold">11. commandeth, and he will smite--</hi>His word of command, when once given, cannot but be fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.11">Is 55:11</reference>). His mere word is enough to smite with destruction.<div eID="gen23242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23243" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">great house ... little house--</hi>He will spare none, great or small (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.15">Am 3:15</reference>). Jerome interprets "the great house" as Israel, and "the small house" as Judah: the former being reduced to branches or ruins, literally, "small drops"; the latter, though injured with "clefts" or rents, which threaten its fall, yet still permitted to stand. <div eID="gen23243" type="x-p"/>
entries.496c8861205c2e883db79e19d7290898399ffd3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12601"/><div sID="gen23244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12601"/>12. In turning "judgment (justice) into gall (poison), and ... righteousness into hemlock" (or wormwood, bitter and noxious), ye act as perversely as if one were to make "horses run upon the rock" or to "plough with oxen there" [Maurer]. As horses and oxen are useless on a rock, so ye are incapable of fulfilling justice [Grotius]. Ye impede the course of God's benefits, because ye are as it were a hard rock on which His favor cannot run. "Those that will not be tilled as fields, shall be abandoned as rocks" [Calvin]. <div eID="gen23244" type="x-p"/>
entries.0afe0911408bcdef27a2360ab9114677398104a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12602"/><div sID="gen23245" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12602"/><hi type="bold">13. rejoice in a thing of naught--</hi>that is, in your vain and fleeting riches.<div eID="gen23245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Have we not taken to us horns--</hi>that is, acquired power, so as to conquer our neighbors (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Ki 14:25</reference>). Horns are the Hebrew symbol of power, being the instrument of strength in many animals (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.10">Psa 75:10</reference>). <div eID="gen23246" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad9b495653371c814152d7ca6f6c939f24ce3a81: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12603"/><div sID="gen23247" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12603"/><hi type="bold">14. from the entering in of Hamath--</hi>the point of entrance for an invading army (as Assyria) into Israel from the north; specified here, as Hamath had been just before subjugated by Jeroboam II (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.2">Am 6:2</reference>). Do not glory in your recently acquired city, for it shall be the starting-point for the foe to afflict you. How sad the contrast to the feast of Solomon attended by a congregation from this same Hamath, the most northern boundary of Israel, to the Nile, the river of Egypt, the most southern boundary!<div eID="gen23247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the river of the wilderness--</hi>that is, to Kedron, which empties itself into the north bay of the Dead Sea below Jericho (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.15">2Ch 28:15</reference>), the southern boundary of the ten tribes (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Ki 14:25</reference>, "from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain") [Maurer]. To the river Nile, which skirts the Arabian wilderness and separates Egypt from Canaan [Grotius]. If this verse includes Judah, as well as Israel (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>, "Zion" and "Samaria"), Grotius' view is correct; and it agrees with <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.65">1Ki 8:65</reference>. <chapter eID="Amos.6"/>

entries.c2c111458960a48a893e2a01fa7209707cdb005f: <div eID="gen34385" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34386" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34387" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34387" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34386" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34388" type="x-p"/> The prophet reproves his people for indulging themselves in luxurious ease, and forming alliances with their powerful idolatrous neighbors, <reference osisRef="Amo.6.1">Amo 6:1</reference>. He asks if their lands or their lot be better than their own, <reference osisRef="Amo.6.2">Amo 6:2</reference>, that they should choose to worship the gods of the heathen, and forsake Jehovah. Then follows an amplification of the sin which the prophet reproves, <reference osisRef="Amo.6.3-Amo.6.6">Amo 6:3-6</reference>; to which he annexes very awful threatenings, confirmed by the oath of Jehovah, <reference osisRef="Amo.6.7">Amo 6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amo.6.8">Amo 6:8</reference>. He next particularly specifies the punishment of their sins by pestilence, <reference osisRef="Amo.6.9-Amo.6.11">Amo 6:9-11</reference>; by famine, or a drought that should harden the earth so that it could not be tilled, <reference osisRef="Amo.6.12">Amo 6:12</reference>; and by the sword of the Assyrians, <reference osisRef="Amo.6.14">Amo 6:14</reference>. <div eID="gen34388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34389" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34390" type="x-p"/> Wo to them that are at ease in Zion - For השאננים hashshaanannim, "who dwell at ease," it has been proposed to read השעננים hashshaanannim, "who confidently lean," the two words differing only in one letter, an ע ain for an א aleph. They leaned confidently on Zion; supposing that, notwithstanding their iniquities they should be saved for Zion's sake. Thus the former clause will agree better with the latter, "leaning upon Zion," and "trusting in the mountain of Samaria." Those that are at ease may mean those who have no concern about the threatened judgments, and who have no deep concern for the salvation of their own souls. Houbigant would read, "Go to them who despise Zion, and trust in Samaria." So the Septuagint, reading שנאים soneim, hating, instead of שאננים shaanannim, being at rest, tranquil Calmet first proposed this conjecture; Houbigant follows him. <div eID="gen34390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34391" type="x-p"/> Are named chief - Newcome renders, "That are named after the chief of the nations;" and observes, that the Hebrew word נקבי nekubey is an allusion to marking a name or character by punctures. See on <reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">Isa 44:5</reference> (note). They call themselves not after their ancestors, but after the chief of the idolatrous nations with whom they intermarry contrary to the law. <div eID="gen34391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34392" type="x-p"/> Perhaps the words here rather refer to the mountains and their temples, than to the people. The mountain of Zion, and the mountain of Samaria, were considered the chief or most celebrated among the nations, as the two kingdoms to which they belonged were the most distinguished on the earth.
entries.133e31e4151abf57acc622641aab49f61d6fa871: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34393" type="x-p"/> Pass ye unto Calneh - This is, says Calmet, the Ctesiphon on the river Tigris. <div eID="gen34393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34394" type="x-p"/> Hamath - The same as Emesa. Hamath was a city on the Orontes, in Syria. <div eID="gen34394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34395" type="x-p"/> Gath - A well-known town, and head of one of the five seignories of the Philistines. <div eID="gen34395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34396" type="x-p"/> Be they better - You have no more reason to expect exemption from the consequences of your sins than they had. They have been punished; so shall you. Why then will ye trust in their gods, that could not save their own cities?
entries.eb60243826bae89c0e1d583cc3348047dd8666ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34397" type="x-p"/> Ye that put far away the evil day - Wo to you who will not consider the day of approaching vengeance; but continue in your iniquity, and harden your hearts. Ye bring your iniquities nearer, and still suppose your punishment to be at a greater distance.
entries.53bcf6691ea64acf5e35f24b28869b3fa318ed4c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34398" type="x-p"/> That lie upon beds of ivory - The word הוי hoi, wo, is understood at the beginning of each of the first, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth verses. The beds mentioned here may be either sofas to recline on at table, or beds to sleep on; and these among the ancients were ornamented with ivory inlaid. They were called lectos eburatos by Plautus, lectos eburnos by Horace, "ivory beds." Probably those ornamented with shells, or mother-of-pearl, may be intended. Several works of this kind may be still seen in Palestine and other places. I have before me a cross brought from Jerusalem, incrusted all over with mother-of-pearl, and various figures chased on it. <div eID="gen34398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34399" type="x-p"/> There must have been a great deal of luxury and effeminacy among the Israelites at this time; and, consequently, abundance of riches. This was in the time of Jeroboam the second, when the kingdom had enjoyed a long peace. The description in the fourth, fifth, and sixth verses, is that of an Asiatic court even in the present day.
entries.ed7ddc89e831d8a05097d67163e51011316990ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34400" type="x-p"/> And invent to themselves instruments of music, like David - See the note on <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.5">1Chr 23:5</reference>; and see especially the note on <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.25">2Chr 29:25</reference> (note). I believe that David was not authorized by the Lord to introduce that multitude of musical instruments into the Divine worship of which we read, and I am satisfied that his conduct in this respect is most solemnly reprehended by this prophet; and I farther believe that the use of such instruments of music, in the Christian Church, is without the sanction and against the will of God; that they are subversive of the spirit of true devotion, and that they are sinful. If there was a wo to them who invented instruments of music, as did David under the law, is there no wo, no curse to them who invent them, and introduce them into the worship of God in the Christian Church? I am an old man, and an old minister; and I here declare that I never knew them productive of any good in the worship of God; and have had reason to believe that they were productive of much evil. Music, as a science, I esteem and admire: but instruments of music in the house of God I abominate and abhor. This is the abuse of music; and here I register my protest against all such corruptions in the worship of the Author of Christianity. The late venerable and most eminent divine, the Revelation John Wesley, who was a lover of music, and an elegant poet, when asked his opinion of instruments of music being introduced into the chapels of the Methodists said, in his terse and powerful manner, "I have no objection to instruments of music in our chapels, provided they are neither Heard nor Seen." I say the same, though I think the expense of purchase had better be spared. <div eID="gen34400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34401" type="x-p"/> The word הפרטים happoretim, which we render chant, and the margin quaver, signifies to dance, to skip, etc. In the sight of such a text, fiddlers, drummers, waltzers, etc., may well tremble, who perform to excite detestable passions.
entries.a57fe7ff1cbef800ad4539fcae769e3d77242a92: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34402" type="x-p"/> That drink wine in bowls - Perhaps the costliness of the drinking vessels, more than the quantity drank, is that which is here reprehended by the prophet. Drinking vessels of the most costly materials, and of the most exquisite workmanship, are still in use; and as to precious ointments and perfumes among the Jews, we have a proof that the contents of one small box was worth three hundred denarii, at least seven pounds ten shillings sterling. See the case in the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Joh.12.5">Joh 12:5</reference> (note), and the note there.
entries.f7d24024ac0d870aafb8708a9aac78ca89ca30e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34403" type="x-p"/> With the first that go captive - The house of Israel shall be carried into captivity before the house of Judah.
entries.44ea6b2f0dc84d3e893fa953327ad24d2c8f7049: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34404" type="x-p"/> The Lord God hath sworn by himself - בנפשו benaphsho, by his soul, his being, existence.
entries.a5f8ee3091a857d6a3a17b9c9cbd6f13aad3fbf1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34405" type="x-p"/> Ten men - they shall die - All shall be cut off by the sword, or by captivity, or by famine.
entries.cd2ad8df57c5989654478da52a85ad7d88c51a3b: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34406" type="x-p"/> A man's uncle shall take him up - Bp. Newcome says, this obscure verse seems to describe the effects of famine and pestilence during the siege of Samaria. The carcass shall be burnt, and the bones removed with no ceremony of funeral rites, and without the assistance of the nearest kinsman. Solitude shall reign in the house; and if one is left, he must be silent, (see <reference osisRef="Amo.8.3">Amo 8:3</reference>), and retired, lest he be plundered of his scanty provision! Burning the body, and then collecting the ashes, and putting them into an urn, was deemed the most honorable mode of burial.
entries.ce906c578d422abd100e6bdb9de94e8e726566c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen34406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34407" type="x-p"/> He will smote the great house with breaches - The great and small shall equally suffer; no distinction shall be made; rich and poor shall fall together; death has received his commission, and he will spare none. Horace has a sentiment precisely like this, Carm. Lib. i., Od. iv., 5:13. <div eID="gen34407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34408" type="x-p"/> Pallida mors aequo pulsat pede pauperum <div eID="gen34408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34409" type="x-p"/> Tabernas, Regumque Turres. <div eID="gen34409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34410" type="x-p"/> With equal pace impartial fate <div eID="gen34410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34411" type="x-p"/> Knocks at the palace as the cottage gate. <div eID="gen34411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34412" type="x-p"/> But this may refer particularly to the houses of the poor in Eastern countries; their mud walls being frequently full of clefts; the earth of which they are built seldom adhering together because of its sandiness.
entries.bd8d05b21153afade2b3fcda8fb7392d8ed694fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34413" type="x-p"/> Shall horses run upon the rock - First, they could not do it, because they were unshod; for the shoeing of horses with iron was not then known. Secondly, If they did run on the rock, it would be useless to their owner, and hurtful to themselves. Thirdly, And it would be as useless to plough on the rock with oxen; for there it would be impossible to sow with any advantage. Fourthly, Just as useless and injurious would it be to put gall in the place of judgment, and hemlock in the place of righteousness. You have not only been laboring in vain for yourselves, but you have also been oppressive to others; and for both ye shall suffer.
entries.d7e1f9d29d0a478ae1c8d0d04c0d63ad245b0c25: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34414" type="x-p"/> Ye which rejoice in a thing of naught - In your idols: for an idol is nothing in the world. <div eID="gen34414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34415" type="x-p"/> Have we not taken to us horns - We have arrived to power and dignity by our strength. Horns were the symbols of power and authority. So Horace: - <div eID="gen34415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34416" type="x-p"/> Vina parant animos: tum pauper cornua sumet. "Wine repairs our strength, and furnishes the poor with horns." <div eID="gen34416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34417" type="x-p"/> At such times they think themselves as great as the greatest.
entries.c4fa3c233ccc47ed5b323165e5928e8303feff04: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen34417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34418" type="x-p"/> I will raise up against you a nation - The Assyrians under Pul, Tiglath-pileser, and Shalmaneser, who subdued the Israelites at various times, and at last carried them away captive in the days of Hosea, the last king of Israel in Samaria. <div eID="gen34418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34419" type="x-p"/> From the entering in of Hamath (on the north) unto the river of the wilderness - Besor, which empties itself into the sea, not far from Gaza, and was in the southern part of the tribe of Simeon.  <chapter eID="Amos.6"/> <div eID="gen34419" type="x-p"/>

entries.ed1689eb95920b0c27ebde857efccc2e5bd37902: <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Amo 6:1</reference> <div eID="gen16398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16399" type="x-p"/> The prophet utters the second woe over the careless heads of the nation, who were content with the existing state of things, who believed in no divine judgment, and who revelled in their riches (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.1-Amos.6.6">Amo 6:1-6</reference>). To these he announces destruction and the general overthrow of the kingdom (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.7-Amos.6.11">Amo 6:7-11</reference>), because they act perversely, and trust in their own power (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.12-Amos.6.14">Amo 6:12-14</reference>). Amo 6:1. <hi type="italic">“Woe to the secure upon Zion, and to the careless upon the mountain of Samaria, to the chief men of the first of the nations, to whom the house of Israel comes!</hi> Amo 6:2. <hi type="italic">Go over to Calneh, and see; and proceed thence to Hamath, the great one: and go down to Gath of the Philistines: are they indeed better than these kingdoms? or is their territory greater than your territory?</hi> Amo 6:3. <hi type="italic">Ye who keep the day of calamity far off, and bring the seat of violence near.” </hi> This woe applies to the great men in Zion and Samaria, that is to say, to the chiefs of the whole of the covenant nation, because they were all sunk in the same godless security; though special allusion is made to the corrupt leaders of the kingdom of the ten tribes, whose debauchery is still further depicted in what follows. These great men are designated in the words נקבי ראשׁית הגּוים, as the heads of the chosen people, who are known by name. As ראשׁית הג is taken from Num 24:20, so נקבי is taken from Num 1:17, where the heads of the tribes who were chosen as princes of the congregation to preside over the numbering of the people are described as men אשׁר נקּבוּ בּשׁמות, who were defined with names, i.e., distinguished by names, that is to say, well-known men; and it is used here in the same sense. Observe, however, with reference to ראשׁית הגּוים, that in Num 24:20 we have not הגּוים, but simply ראשׁית גּוים. Amalek is so called there, as being the first heathen nation which rose up in hostility to Israel. On the other hand, ר הגוים is the firstling of the nations, i.e., the first or most exalted of all nations. Israel is so called, because Jehovah had chosen it out of all the nations of the earth to be the people of His possession (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Exo 19:5</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.23">2Sa 7:23</reference>). In order to define with still greater precision the position of these princes in the congregation, Amos adds, “to whom the house of Israel cometh,” namely, to have its affairs regulated by them as its rulers. These epithets were intended to remind the princes of the people of both kingdoms, “that they were the descendants of those tribe-princes who had once been honoured to conduct the affairs of the chosen family, along with Moses and Aaron, and whose light shone forth from that better age as brilliant examples of what a truly theocratical character was” (Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Dissertations</hi>, i. p. 148). To give still greater prominence to the exalted calling of these princes, Amos shows in <reference osisRef="Amos.6.2">Amo 6:2</reference> that Israel can justly be called the firstling of the nations, since it is not inferior either in prosperity or greatness to any of the powerful and prosperous heathen states. Amos names three great and flourishing capitals, because he is speaking to the great men of the capitals of the two kingdoms of Israel, and the condition of the whole kingdom is reflected in the circumstances of the capital. <hi type="italic">Calneh</hi> (= <hi type="italic">Calno</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.9">Isa 10:9</reference>) is the later <hi type="italic">Ctesiphon</hi> in the land of Shinar, or Babylonia, situated upon the Tigris opposite to Seleucia (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">Gen 10:10</reference>); hence the expression עברוּ, because men were obliged to cross over the river (Euphrates) in order to get there. <hi type="italic">Hamath</hi>: the capital of the Syrian kingdom of that name, situated upon the Orontes (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.10.18">Gen 10:18</reference> and Num 34:8). There was not another Hamath, as Hitzig supposes. The circumstance that Amos mentions Calneh first, whereas it was much farther to the east, so that Hamath was nearer to Palestine than Calneh was, may be explained very simply, from the fact that the enumeration commences with the most distant place and passes from the north-east to the south-west, which was in the immediate neighbourhood of Israel. <hi type="italic">Gath</hi>: one of the five capitals of Philistia, and in David’s time the capital of all Philistia (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">2Sa 8:1</reference>). The view still defended by Baur - namely, that Amos mentions here three cities that had either lost their former grandeur, or had fallen altogether, for the purpose of showing the self-secure princes of Israel that the same fate awaited Zion and Samaria - is groundless and erroneous; for although <hi type="italic">Calneh</hi> is spoken of in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.9">Isa 10:9</reference> as a city that had been conquered by the Assyrians, it cannot be proved that this was the case as early as the time of Amos, but is a simple inference drawn from a false interpretation of the verse before us. Nor did Jeroboam II conquer the city of Hamath on the Orontes, and incorporate its territory with his own kingdom (see at 2Ki 14:25). And although the Philistian city <hi type="italic">Gath</hi> was conquered by Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:60, we cannot infer from <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.6">2Ch 26:6</reference>, or from the fact of Gath not being mentioned in <reference osisRef="Amos.1.6-Amos.1.8">Amo 1:6-8</reference>, that this occurred before the time of Amos (see at <reference osisRef="Amos.1.8">Amo 1:8</reference>). On the other hand, the fact that it is placed by the side of Hamath in the passage before us, is rather a proof that the conquest did not take place till afterwards.
entries.a2e7dd371b29e38e79b2032041ed7b5d58ccf20e: <reference osisRef="Amos.6.2-Amos.6.3">Amo 6:2-3</reference> <div eID="gen16399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16400" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Amos.6.2">Amo 6:2</reference> states what the princes of Israel are to see in the cities mentioned, - namely, that they are not better off (טובים denoting outward success or earthly prosperity) than these two kingdoms, i.e., the kingdoms of Judah and Israel, and that their territories are not larger than theirs. It is very evident that this does not apply to cities that have been destroyed. The double question ה ... אם requires a negative answer. Amo 6:3. assigns the reason for the woe pronounced upon the sinful security of the princes of Israel, by depicting the godless conduct of these princes; and this is appended in the manner peculiar to Amos, viz., in participles. These princes fancy that the evil day, i.e., the day of misfortune or of judgment and punishment, is far away (מנדּים, <hi type="italic">piel</hi> of נדה = נדד, to be far off, signifies in this instance not to put far away, but to regard as far off); and they go so far as to prepare a seat or throne close by for wickedness and violence, which must be followed by judgment. הגּישׁ שׁבת, to move the sitting (<hi type="italic">shebheth</hi> from <hi type="italic">yâshabh</hi>) of violence near, or better still, taking <hi type="italic">shebheth</hi> in the sense of enthroning, as Ewald does, to move the throne of violence nearer, i.e., to cause violence to erect its throne nearer and nearer among them.
entries.82105a877071a52a9b90b70d9e9ed1daf17a6ae4: <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4-Amos.6.6">Amo 6:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen16400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16401" type="x-p"/> This forgetfulness of God shows itself more especially in the reckless licentiousness and debauchery of these men. Amo 6:4. <hi type="italic">“They who lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat lambs from the flock, and calves out of the fattening stall.</hi> Amo 6:5. <hi type="italic">Who prattle to the tune of the harp; like David, they invent string instruments.</hi> Amo 6:6. <hi type="italic">Who drink wine out of sacrificial bowls, and anoint themselves with the best oils, and do not afflict themselves for the hurt of Joseph.” </hi> They lie stretched, as it were poured out (סרחים), upon beds inlaid with ivory, to feast and fill their belly with the flesh of the best lambs and fattened calves, to the playing of harps and singing, in which they take such pleasure, that they invent new kinds of playing and singing. The ἁπ. λεγ. <hi type="italic">pârat</hi>, to strew around (cf. <hi type="italic">peret</hi> in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.10">Lev 19:10</reference>), in Arabic to throw many useless words about, to gossip, describes the singing at the banquets as frivolous nonsense. כּלי שׁיר, articles or instruments of singing, are not musical instruments generally, but, as we may see from <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.12">2Ch 34:12</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.26-2Chr.29.27">2Ch 29:26-27</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.5">1Ch 23:5</reference>, the stringed instruments that were either invented by David (e.g., the <hi type="italic">nebel</hi>), or arranged by him for the sacred song of the temple, together with the peculiar mode of playing them; in other words, “the playing upon stringed instruments introduced by David.” Consequently the meaning of <reference osisRef="Amos.6.5">Amo 6:5</reference> is the following: As David invented stringed instruments in honour of his God in heaven, so do these princes invent playing and singing for their god, the belly. The meaning to invent or devise, which Baur will not allow to חשׁב, is established beyond all doubt by Exo 31:4. They drink thereby out of sacrificial bowls of wine, i.e., drink wine out of sacrificial bowls. שׁתה with ב, as in Gen 44:5. <hi type="italic">Mizrâq</hi>, in the plural <hi type="italic">mizrâqı̄m</hi> and <hi type="italic">mizrâqōth</hi>, from <hi type="italic">zâraq</hi>, to sprinkle, was the name given both to the vessels used for the sprinkling of the blood, and also to the bowls made use of for pouring the libation of wine upon the table of shew-bread (<reference osisRef="2Chr.4.8">2Ch 4:8</reference>). This word is applied by Amos to the bowls out of which the gluttons drank their wine; with special reference to the offering of silver sacrificial bowls made by the tribe-princes at the consecration of the altar (Numbers 7), to show that whereas the tribe-princes of Israel in the time of Moses manifested their zeal for the service of Jehovah by presenting sacrificial bowls of silver, the princes of his own time showed just as much zeal in their care for their god, the belly. <hi type="italic">Mizrâqı̄m</hi> does not mean “rummers, or pitchers used for mixing wine.” Lastly, Amos refers to their anointing themselves with the firstling of the oils, i.e., the best oils, as a sign of unbridled rejoicing, inasmuch as the custom of anointing was suspended in time of mourning (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.2">2Sa 14:2</reference>), for the purpose of appending the antithesis ולא גחלוּ, they do not afflict or grieve themselves for the ruin of Israel. <hi type="italic">Shēbher</hi>, breach, injury, destruction. <hi type="italic">Joseph</hi> signifies the people and kingdom of the ten tribes.
entries.b9b534fc218b3c4083ad3688b43816d8aabd6e52: <reference osisRef="Amos.6.7">Amo 6:7</reference> <div eID="gen16401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16402" type="x-p"/> Announcement of Punishment. - Amo 6:7. <hi type="italic">“Therefore will they now go into captivity at the head of the captives, and the shouting of the revellers will depart.” </hi> Because these revellers do not trouble themselves about the ruin of Israel, they will now be obliged to wander into captivity at the head of the people (cf. 1Ki 21:9), when the approaching <hi type="italic">shebher</hi> occurs. בּראשׁ גּלים is chosen with direct reference to ראשׁית שׁמנים, as Jerome has observed: “Ye who are <hi type="italic">first</hi> in riches will be the <hi type="italic">first</hi> to bear the yoke of captivity.” <hi type="italic">Serūchı̄m</hi> also points back to <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4">Amo 6:4</reference>, “those who are stretched upon their couches” - that is, the revellers; and it forms a play upon words with <hi type="italic">mirzach</hi>. מרזח signifies a loud cry, here a joyous cry, in <reference osisRef="Jer.16.5">Jer 16:5</reference> a cry of lamentation.
entries.5398d6500f2bcfa34ef6b7eaa3eaea1fb32ceb65: <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8-Amos.6.11">Amo 6:8-11</reference> <div eID="gen16402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16403" type="x-p"/> This threat is carried out still further in <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Amo 6:8</reference>-11. Amo 6:8. <hi type="italic">“The Lord Jehovah hath sworn by Himself, is the saying of Jehovah, the God of hosts: I abhor the pride of Jacob, and his palaces I hate; and give up the city, and the fulness thereof.</hi> Amo 6:9. <hi type="italic">And it will come to pass, if then men are left in a house, they shall die.</hi> Amo 6:10. <hi type="italic">And when his cousin lifts him up, and he that burieth him, to carry out the bones out of the house, and saith to the one in the hindermost corner of the house, Is there still any one with thee? and he says, Not one; then will he say, Hush; for the name of Jehovah is not to be invoked.</hi> Amo 6:11. <hi type="italic">For, behold, Jehovah commandeth, and men smite the great house to ruins, and the small house into shivers.” </hi> In order to show the secure debauchees the terrible severity of the judgments of God, the Lord announces to His people with a solemn oath the rejection of the nation which is so confident in its own power (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.6.13">Amo 6:13</reference>). The oath runs here as in <reference osisRef="Amos.4.2">Amo 4:2</reference>, with this exception, that instead of בּקדשׁו we have בּנפשׁו in the same sense; for the <hi type="italic">nephesh</hi> of Jehovah, His inmost being or self, is His holiness. מתאב, with the guttural softened, for מתעב. The participle describes the abhorrence as a continued lasting feeling, and not a merely passing emotion. גּאון יעקב, the loftiness or pride of Jacob, i.e., everything of which Jacob is proud, the true and imaginary greatness and pride of Israel, which included the palaces of the voluptuous great men, for which reason they are placed in parallelism with גאון יע. This glory of Israel Jehovah abhors, and He will destroy it by giving up the city (Samaria), and all that fills it (houses and men), to the enemies to be destroyed. גאון יע, to give up to the enemy, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">Deu 32:30</reference> and Oba 1:14; not to surround, to which וּמלאהּ is unsuitable. The words not only threaten surrounding, or siege, but also conquest, and (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.11">Amo 6:11</reference>) the destruction of the city. And then, even if there are ten in one house, they will all perish. אנשׁים: people, men. Ten in one house is a large number, which the prophet assumes as the number, to give the stronger emphasis to the thought that not one will escape from death. This thought is still further explained in Amo 6:10. A relative comes into the house to bury his deceased blood-relation. The suffix to נשׂאו refers to the idea involved in מתוּ, a dead man. <hi type="italic">Dōd</hi>, literally the father’s brother, here any near relation whose duty it was to see to the burial of the dead. מסרף for משׂרף, the burner, i.e., the burier of the dead. The Israelites were indeed accustomed to <hi type="italic">bury</hi> their dead, and not to <hi type="italic">burn</hi> the corpses. The description of the burier as <hi type="italic">mesârēph</hi> (a burner) therefore supposes the occurrence of such a multitude of deaths that it is impossible to bury the dead, whose corpses are obliged to be burned, for the purpose of preventing the air from being polluted by the decomposition of the corpses. Of course the burning did not take place at the house, as Hitzig erroneously infers from להוציא עצמים; for עצמים denotes the corpse here, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.13.19">Exo 13:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.24.32">Jos 24:32</reference>, and 2Ki 13:21, and not the different bones of the dead which remained without decomposition or burning. The burier now asks the last living person in the house, who has gone to the very back of the house in order to save his life, whether there is any one still with him, any one still living in the house beside himself, and receives the answer, אפס (Adv.), “Nothing more;” whereupon he says to him, <hi type="italic">has</hi>, “Be still,” answering to our Hush! because he is afraid that, if he goes on speaking, he may invoke the name of God, or pray for the mercy of God; and he explains his words by adding, “The name of Jehovah must not be mentioned.” It is not Amos who adds this explanation, but the relation. Nor does it contain “the words of one who despairs of any better future, and whose mind is oppressed by the weight of the existing evils, as if he said, Prayers would be of no use, for we too must die” (Lievl., Ros.). לא להזכּיר, “it is not to (may not) be mentioned,” would be unsuitable as an utterance of despair. It rather indicates the fear lest, by the invocation of the name of God, the eye of God should be drawn towards this last remaining one, and he also should fall a victim to the judgment of death. This judgment the Lord accomplishes not merely by a pestilence which breaks out during the siege, and rages all around (there is no ground for any such limitation of the words), but also by sword and plague during the siege and conquest of the town. For the reason assigned for the threat in <reference osisRef="Amos.6.11">Amo 6:11</reference> points to the latter. כּי links the words to the main thought in <reference osisRef="Amos.6.11">Amo 6:11</reference>, or even <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Amos.6.10">Amo 6:10</reference></hi>: “When the Lord delivers up the city and all that fills it, they will all perish; for, behold, He commands, orders the enemy (the nation in <reference osisRef="Amos.6.14">Amo 6:14</reference>), and it will smite in pieces the houses, great and small.” The singular הבּית is used with indefinite generality: every house, great and small (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.3.15">Amo 3:15</reference>).
entries.0101f074cbc9edaf350381109b4488664eec4f14: <reference osisRef="Amos.6.12-Amos.6.14">Amo 6:12-14</reference> <div eID="gen16403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16404" type="x-p"/> This judgment also, they, with their perversion of all right, will be unable to avert by their foolish trust in their own power.
